edges.effect_quant: In Denmark, oral antibiotics during the first 5 years of life were associated with pediatric-onset IBD (HR 1.33, 95% CI 1.2-1.5) in 1927 cases and 18,318 reference individuals; in Norway, antibiotic exposure before age 2 carried an aOR of 1.33 (95% CI 1.15-1.53), rising to 1.47 after more than two courses and 2.57 for broad-spectrum exposure.
edges.population: children exposed to systemic antibiotics in infancy or early childhood, especially large Scandinavian registry cohorts assessing pediatric-onset inflammatory bowel disease
edges.mechanism: Antibiotics in early life can disrupt microbiome maturation, deplete key commensals, alter bile acid and short-chain fatty acid ecology, and potentially skew mucosal immune development toward later chronic intestinal inflammation.
edges.summary: Across large pediatric registry cohorts, early-life antibiotic exposure tracks with a higher later risk of pediatric IBD, especially Crohn disease and repeated or broad-spectrum exposure. The effect is modest in relative terms but appears consistent enough to support a harmful population-level signal.
edges.caveats: Absolute risk remains low, and residual confounding by infections, healthcare utilization, and underlying susceptibility is still possible. The evidence is observational, so it supports stewardship rather than a claim that brief necessary antibiotic treatment directly causes IBD in any given child.
